steps: Permit & plan the layout
Check restrictions and permits with the authority having jurisdiction. Plan the fireplace, chimney and options together; avoid cutting joists, and keep the chimney inside or in an insulated chase.

No special floor reinforcement is needed. Remove the door until all finishing work is done, to protect it from gypsum dust, muriatic acid, plaster, cement and paint.

  • A cold chimney causes poor draft: run it inside if possible, or enclose it in an insulated chase.
  • Many options need wiring or electricity. If any may be added later, run suitable wiring during framing.
  • The framing examples are shown only as a dimensioned drawing (Figure 2) and are larger than required. A Clean Face needs an extra 12" on the left for the intake air duct, the Heat Dump Option an extra 12" on its side, and Central Heat extra space on top and maybe one side.
Never install an insert, a gas log set (vented or unvented) or a gas log lighter in this fireplace, and don't install a flue damper.

RSF strongly recommends installation and service by professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).
Mobile home restrictions
Vented roof flashing and outside combustion air are mandatory. No gravity vents, central heat or Clean Face, and never in a sleeping room.

• Use a vented roof flashing.
  • Use outside air as combustion air, and make sure nothing blocks the inlet.
  • Gravity vents, the central heating system and the Clean Face option are not allowed.
  • Do not install in sleeping rooms.
  • Provide access openings to the fireplace and chimney enclosures so the installation and clearances can be inspected after any move.
  • Install a radiation shield at each floor the chimney passes through; the ICC part extends to the outermost plane of the roof.
  • Offset through the wall: check with the authority having jurisdiction whether the chimney must be enclosed outside.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, walls and ceiling/roof.
Ceiling height & enclosure vents

Fireplace base to lowest ceiling point: 7' min. in a sealed enclosure, 6' in a vented one, inside and outside the enclosure. Venting means 3"x10" grilles or larger in holes within 1' of the floor and the ceiling.
Install the standoffs

Before setting the unit, screw both side standoffs and the top standoff (back shield bent to 45°, centered) to the casing with front returns aligned to the facing. Seal the ¼" gap with silicone and fill nothing behind it.
Secure to the floor
Fasten the casing or base to the floor with the four crate brackets, placed as they were on the crate; if possible, at least one into a floor joist with 2" wood screws.
Outside air duct
Insulated aluminium flex duct rated over 200° F: 4" for total runs under 25', 5" beyond. Max 12' vertical rise; inlet at least 5' below the rain cap and never in an attic.

1. Choose the inlet location, above or below floor level.
  2. Cut a 4 ¼" hole in the outside wall (5 ¼" for 5" duct), push the inlet in from outside and seal it to the wall.
  3. At each end, pull back the insulation and plastic cover, screw the duct to the inlet sleeve and the fireplace connecting sleeve, then re-cover it and tape with 2" aluminium duct tape.

Both 4" and 5" connecting sleeves come with the fireplace; RSF suggests its 4" outside air kit (FO-INT). Don't crimp the duct at corners. Looping the duct makes an optional cold air trap.
Louvers or Clean Face
Mandatory: install the louvers (FO-F320SBRLB), or the Clean Face (FO-F2) with its intake duct plus two gravity vent kits (FO-V2 or FO-V3).

Leaving out the Clean Face intake duct or either gravity vent will overheat the unit and may put safety at risk. Gravity vent dampers can't be installed on a Clean Face.

  • Each gravity vent kit includes 5' of insulated flexible ducting; add 5' lengths with FO-DUCT5, up to 15' maximum.
  • The internal blower (FO-HB9) is for the Louvered fireplace, the inline fan (FO-CIF) for the Clean Face. Central Heat on a Clean Face needs the Central Heat T (FO-T).
  • RSF recommends no electrical options or thermal switch inside a Clean Face; the non-combustible finish may have to be broken to service them.

Which options are required, optional or not available for each version is shown only as a check-mark table (p. 27).
EXCEL chimney
7" ICC EXCEL only. Frame 13" square openings, fit a radiation shield at every floor, keep 2" to combustibles, and fix the first length with the three screws provided.

1. Frame 13" square rough openings in floors, ceilings and roof (slightly bigger is fine, never smaller).
  2. From below, install a radiation shield at each floor; in the attic, a radiation shield and a storm collar. Cathedral ceiling: XM-7ERSC.
  3. Secure the first length to the fireplace with the three screws provided, then assemble the rest. The fireplace can support up to 18' of chimney; see the EXCEL manual for supports and bracing.
  4. Extend at least 3' above the roof contact point and 2' higher than any wall, roof or building within 10'. More than 5' above the roof needs a roof brace.
  5. Roof radiation shield (XM-7ERRS), extending 1" above the roof line.
  6. Flashing: vented if the chimney is enclosed to the roof, regular if not. Seal it to the roof with roofing tar, under the upper shingles and over the lower ones, and nail it with roofing nails.
  7. Seal the storm collar to the chimney with silicone (not roofing tar), then fit and secure the rain cap.
Keep 2" or more between the chimney and combustibles, and don't fill that space with insulation.

Offsets

Max 30° in the USA (45° in Canada) and four elbows (two offsets and returns). An elbow may sit directly on the fireplace. Three screws per joint, and a wall or offset support above each offset. Through an exterior wall, use an angled wall insulated radiation shield (XM-7EWRSI30 or XM-7EWRSI45).
Non-combustible facing
Face with non-combustible material only, such as metal, brick, slate, ceramic tile or painted cement board. Gypsum board is not acceptable and can't come closer than the side and top standoffs.

Ceramic tile can be glued on with high temperature silicone sealant. The rock retainer kit (FO-KFSBR) simplifies thin materials such as ceramic tile or sliced brick; it isn't designed or required for full brick or stone, and thin materials can also go straight on the face with high temperature silicone. On a Louvered fireplace, leave the black metal completely exposed or completely covered.
Hearth, spark guard & mantel
Non-combustible hearth at least 20" deep and 42" wide, centered on the opening; spark guard half under the fireplace unless the floor is non-combustible; combustible mantel per Table 2.

panels.title: Smoke when the door opens
items: Door opened too quickly → open it more slowly
Dirty chimney or plugged cap → screened caps clog with creosote
Chimney too short for the altitude or number of elbows → see Table 3
Central heat or internal blower running → turn it off before opening
Range hood or bathroom fan depressurizing the house → open a nearby window a little
Too little kindling → build a hot fire quickly

panels.title: Burns excessively fast
items: Air leaking past door seals or gaskets → paper test, adjust or replace the gasket
Hole in a secondary air tube at the top of the firebox
Excessive draft → hotter fire, shorter burn times
Poorly adjusted door → over-firing, excessive wood consumption

panels.title: Weak draft or hard to light
items: Smoke entering the room, difficulty lighting or operating
Often mistaken for a blocked air intake → adding chimney height is the most common fix
Cold chimney run outside → enclose it in an insulated chase
Wet wood → hard to burn, more creosote, dark glass

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
There's no air knob to set. The air control is automatic, so lighting is all about the kindling and the door.

  1. Lay crumpled newspaper as your fire starter. Use enough to light the kindling (5-6 pieces should do).
  2. Lay 3 or 4 layers of kindling crisscrossed over the paper. Plenty of kindling heats the chimney quickly and builds a strong draft.
  3. Light the paper. Close the door most of the way, leaving it about 1" open. You should see air rushing in.
  4. Once the kindling is burning on its own, add small pieces of seasoned cordwood, always at least 3. Use the andirons so the wood doesn't flatten the fire, and leave air gaps between pieces.
  5. Leave the door slightly open until the wood catches, about 3-5 minutes. Then close it completely.

Some soot on the glass during light-up is normal. It should burn off as the fireplace heats up.

Never use flammable liquids to start a fire. Don't use a grate or raise the fire. Keep the fire behind the andirons, and move any log that falls against the glass.

reload.title: Adding wood
reload.html:
Have your next load ready before you open the door. The firebox cools quickly while the door is open, but don't rush.

  1. Turn off the central heat and internal blowers, if you have them. Running blowers can push smoke out of the fireplace.
  2. Open the door slowly so smoke doesn't spill into the room.
  3. Poke and stir the unburnt wood to revive the fire, then add the new logs.
  4. Keep a clear path in front of the pilot, the metal tube centered between the two andiron posts. It brings air close to the coals.
  5. Leave the door slightly ajar for about 3-10 minutes, depending on how dry the wood is and how many coals were left. Close it once the new wood is well lit.
  6. Wait at least 15 minutes after closing the door before you turn any blowers back on.
Smoke spilling out? Check that kitchen and bathroom fans are off. They can pull smoke out of the fireplace.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
This fireplace burns best with seasoned cordwood.

  • Seasoned means cut, split and dried under cover for at least 6 months, preferably a year or more. Dry seasoned wood generally has less than 20% moisture.
  • Wet wood is hard to burn. It lowers efficiency, builds creosote and leaves dark deposits on the glass. You can burn a lot of it and get very little heat.
  • Hardwoods burn longer and more evenly. All wood gives about the same heat per pound, but more weight of hardwood fits in the firebox.

Never burn

Unseasoned wood, driftwood, treated wood, coal, colored paper, cardboard, trash, garbage or plastic. Don't rely on construction scraps (2x4 or plywood) as your only fuel, and don't burn large amounts of paper, cardboard or mill ends. They can over-fire and damage the fireplace.

Firelogs: wax logs aren't recommended because they dirty the glass. If you use wax or densified firelogs, burn only one at a time and don't poke or stir it. Use only firelogs evaluated for fireplace use.

glass.title: Glass, door seal & finish
glass.html:
The glass

A good hot fire once a day usually burns off most deposits. The drier the wood and the hotter the fire, the cleaner the glass.

  • Clean it only when it's cool. Hot glass can cause a serious burn.
  • Never use an abrasive cleaner. Use a cleaner your dealer recommends; wood stove glass cleaners work far better than regular glass or oven cleaners.
  • Heat won't break the glass, but impact can. Don't slam the door.

The painted finish

Wipe it with a soft damp cloth and mild detergent. Don't spray glass cleaner on the paint, because it may remove it. For touch-ups, use Stove Bright Metallic Black high temperature paint on a cold fireplace, with the room well ventilated.

The door seal

Latch the door on a sheet of paper and pull gently. If the paper tears or is hard to pull out, the seal is good. Check every side. If a worn or damaged gasket fails this test, replace it; kits are available from your RSF dealer. Don't over-tighten the latch every time. That wears out the gasket and strains the handle.

first.title: Your first few fires
first.html:
A slow start

The first few fires start slowly. The refractory bricks lining the firebox hold moisture from manufacturing, and it takes a few hot fires to dry them out.

Black bricks that turn white

While the bricks are still damp, they look black with smoke deposits. Once the moisture is gone, they turn white.

No break-in needed

Unlike a cast iron stove, this fireplace doesn't need curing with small fires first. Feel free to light a large fire from the very start.

A smell, maybe the smoke alarm

Expect a slight odor during the first few fires as the paint cures and oil burns off the metal. It may be strong enough to set off your smoke detector. Open the doors and windows to air out the room.

Dark glass while a fire gets going is normal too. It should burn off as the fireplace heats up.

heat.title: Heat & air control
heat.html:
You won't find an air knob. The combustion air control is fully automatic, and there's no user access to it.

How it works

A bi-metallic coil lets in more air when the fireplace is cold and less as it heats up. The fire burns quickly at light-up, then gradually slows down for the best efficiency and lower emissions. This saves wood and keeps the firebox from overheating.

Getting more or less heat

Use one or two logs at a time for a smaller fire, or more logs for more heat. Don't tamper with the air control.

Outside air

The fireplace is designed to burn outside air, and RSF recommends always using it. A sliding door behind the bottom louver, below the firebox, picks the source: push it toward the back for outside air, or pull it toward the front for room air.

In a mobile home, you must use outside air.

smoke.title: Smoke in the room or a runaway fire
smoke.html:
Smoke comes in when you open the door

  • Open the door more slowly. Opening it fast pulls smoke into the room.
  • Turn off the central heat kit or internal blower before you open the door.
  • Check for other fans running, especially a kitchen range hood or bathroom exhaust fan.
  • Open a window near the fireplace a little to equalize the pressure. Close it once the draft is going.
  • Use enough kindling to get a hot fire quickly. Lighting is when smoke is most likely to get in.
  • Make sure the chimney is clean and the cap isn't plugged. Caps with screens clog more easily with creosote.
  • Make sure the chimney is tall enough for your altitude and number of elbows.

The fire burns too fast and won't slow down

  • Check the door seals and gaskets for air leaks with the paper test (see the glass and door seal tips).
  • Inspect the secondary air tubes at the top of the firebox. A hole lets in unwanted air.
Over-firing: if you can't slow the fire down, or the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red, you're over-firing the fireplace.

chimney.title: Chimney, creosote & ashes
chimney.html:
Slow fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire.

Check and sweep

  • Check the chimney for creosote every week or so until you learn how often it needs cleaning.
  • Clean it once the buildup reaches 1/8" (3 mm). Soot or creosote thicker than that means clean it right away; you may also need to change how you burn and check more often.
  • Close the fireplace door before sweeping. Use a 7" round brush.
  • Leave the baffle in place. Vacuum its top metal plate after sweeping, but keep the nozzle away from the soft white insulation at the sides and back. It tears easily.

Ashes

Empty the ashes before they get deep enough to spill when you open the door. Put them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Set the closed container on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, and keep the ashes in it until all cinders have thoroughly cooled.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• Keep furniture, firewood and anything else that can burn at least 4' from the front of the fireplace.
  • Have at least one smoke detector on each level of the house and at least one carbon monoxide detector.
  • Run the fireplace with the door fully closed. A partly open door can draw gas and flame out of the opening. Leave it ajar only as the lighting and reloading steps describe.
  • Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Keep them well away while it's in use.
  • Don't use a grate or any product not specified for this fireplace. Never add an insert, a gas log set or a gas log lighter.
  • Don't tamper with the automatic air control, and don't add a flue damper.
  • The fireplace needs periodic inspection and repair. RSF strongly recommends professionals certified by the National Fireplace Institute (U.S.) or Wood Energy Technology Transfer Inc. (Canada).
Signs of over-firing: you can't slow down the burn rate, or the chimney connector behind the top louver glows red. Don't over-fire the fireplace.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
RSF warrants its fireplaces against defects in material and workmanship for 30 years, with coverage that steps down over time:

Year 1Defective parts repaired or replaced, plus reasonable labor
Years 2 to 5Parts repaired or replaced; no labor
Years 6 to 30Replacement parts, if available, at 50% of the published retail price; no labor
Electrical componentsOne year only

Not covered

  • Glass and andirons
  • Normal wear and tear, such as paint discoloration, worn gaskets, and eroded or cracked refractory
  • Vandalism, neglect, abuse, over-firing, improper fuel or fuel loads, or failing to service the unit
  • Repairs not authorized by RSF in advance, freight for replacement parts, and damage in transit
  • Installations that don't meet the manual's requirements
The warranty isn't transferable. Defective parts go back through an authorized RSF dealer, and non-genuine parts void the warranty. This is a summary; the full terms are in the manual.

specPerf.title: Emissions, efficiency & heat output
specPerf.html:
EPA 2020 particulate standard (crib wood)1.4 grams per hour
Efficiency65.9%
Maker's website: Optimal Efficiency 75% (LHV); EPA Average Efficiency 66% (HHV).
Maximum heat output22 563 BTU/hr
Maker's website: BTU Output 22,563 BTU/h, based on EPA certification testing using crib wood and calculations from CSA B415.1-10. BTU Maximum 50,000 BTU/h, based on engineering calculations using firebox volume, efficiency, loading density (12lb/cu ft for hardwood), average humidity, reloading interval, type of installation, etc.

Lab results based on the higher heating value of the wood, crib wood EPA emission test data and CSA B415.1:22 calculations. Field results vary with the type of installation, chimney height and cordwood used.

The burn rate is set at the factory by the automatic bi-metallic air control; there is no user access to it. The listing label is glued to the bottom of the fireplace below the floor shield: remove the bottom louver to read it.

Masonry chimney: run EXCEL from the fireplace to a listed stainless-steel liner (EXCEL, or listed to ULC-S635, ULC-S640 or UL-1777) fitted inside the clay liner to the top, joined with masonry adaptor FO-FDM7. An existing masonry chimney must first be inspected by the authority having jurisdiction and serve this fireplace only.

specFlue.title: Minimum recommended flue heights
specFlue.html:
Measured from the top of the fireplace to the top of the chimney before installing the rain cap. Add approximately 6" of minimum height for every 1000' of elevation; every offset (one pair of elbows) adds more.

Columns: straight · 1 x 15° · 2 x 15° · 1 x 30° · 2 x 30°

0 - 1000 ft12' · 13' · 14' · 15' · 18'
1001 - 2000 ft12'6" · 13'6" · 14'6" · 15'6" · 19'
2001 - 3000 ft13' · 14' · 15' · 16' · 19'6"
3001 - 4000 ft13'6" · 14'6" · 15'6" · 17' · 20'
4001 - 5000 ft14' · 15' · 16' · 17'6" · 21'
5001 - 6000 ft14'6" · 15'6" · 17' · 18' · 21'6"
6001 - 7000 ft15' · 16' · 17'6" · 18'6" · 22'
7001 - 8000 ft15'6" · 16'6" · 18' · 19' · 23'
8001 - 9000 ft16' · 17' · 18'6" · 20' · 24'

With two different offsets, use the two-offset column for the bigger pair of elbows. Manual example: at 6015', a straight chimney needs at least 15'; with one 30° offset, at least 18'6".

The table's 45° columns aren't shown here: 45° elbows are not allowed in the USA (Canada allows up to 45°).

specClear.html:

specHearth.title: Hearth extension & spark guard
specHearth.html:
Hearth depth, from the front of the fireplace20" min.
Hearth width, centered on the opening42" min.
Hearth thicknessno minimum
Spark guard provided5" x 36" sheet metal
Spark guard width36" min.

Hearth: non-combustible material such as brick, tile, stone or slate. Spark guard: half under the fireplace (it extends 2½" beneath it) and half under the hearth extension, centered on the door opening; not required on a non-combustible floor.

Raised installations need a site-built guard: Z-shaped when the base is 2 ½" or less above the hearth flooring (as tall as that gap, at least 2½" under both), right-angle when higher (sides at least 2½" x 2½", covered with non-combustible material).

The factory floor shield under the firebox must never be removed. It is only modified to install the internal blower; extend it again if the blower is ever removed.

specMantel.title: Combustible mantel
specMantel.html:
Shelf 0" to 6" deep20" above top of firebox opening

Measured to the bottom of the combustible mantel, and never lower than 20" above the opening. Manual example: a 9¼" shelf needs (9.25 – 6) + 20 = 23¼". On a variable-depth shelf, neither the widest part nor the lowest point may sit below the minimum height for its depth.

Mantel posts beside the opening must be non-combustible unless they meet the 12" side-wall clearance. Non-combustible mantels can go anywhere that doesn't block the louvers; if one sits below the combustible-mantel height, cover the wall between it and the facing with non-combustible material.

review.notes: One combined owner's / installation manual; the manual names the model FOCUS 320 SBR (catalog name FOCUS SBR). Shown only as drawings or images, so not transcribed: unit dimensions (Figure 1, p. 6), framing examples (Figure 2, p. 12; only its text notes about extra space for Clean Face, Heat Dump and Central Heat are used), installation and chimney drawings (pp. 13-14, 16, 18-21), complete options list (pp. 25-26), configured options check-mark table (p. 27), replacement parts (pp. 28-29) and the listing label itself (p. 24). The manual text gives no firebox volume, maximum log length, weight, heating area, view or glass area, or unit dimensions, so those catalog specs could not be checked; the catalog height, width and depth equal numbers in the Figure 2 framing drawing, which the manual says is larger than required. Catalog emissions (1.4 g/hr), EPA output (22 563 BTU/hr), 7 in flue, optional blower, outside air, mobile home approval and 30-year warranty match the manual. No safety listing standard (UL/ULC) is named in the text; the certification line uses the 2020 EPA emission statement on p. 4. Door position: p. 3 says to operate with the door fully closed, while lighting (p. 9) and refueling (pp. 9-10) leave it ajar for a few minutes; both are presented together rather than flagged as a conflict. Spark guard (p. 22): the provided piece is 5" x 36" and the text says it can be cut to the 36" minimum width; odd but not contradictory, so the cutting remark is left out. Two internal cross-references use wrong printed page numbers: p. 15 sends readers to Troubleshooting 'on page 8' (printed page 9, physical p. 10) and p. 4 to the configured option list 'on page 24' (printed page 26, physical p. 27). Table 3 (p. 17) is transcribed for the straight, 15 and 30 degree columns; the 45 degree columns are omitted because 45 degree elbows are not allowed in the USA. Faults come from the troubleshooting section (p. 10) plus the draft (p. 8), fuel (p. 9), door adjustment (p. 11) and location (p. 12) text; there is no code table. Refractory brick and baffle replacement (p. 23) are not covered beyond the sweeping advice. The table of contents has garbled 'ti' ligatures only; no French or offset-font text. Website comparison (Oct 12, website.json): BTU Maximum 50,000 BTU/h and Optimal Efficiency 75% (LHV) differ from the manual's 22 563 BTU/hr and 65.9% (HHV), and EPA Average Efficiency 66% (HHV) is the manual's 65.9% rounded; both website BTU rows and both efficiency rows are quoted in small notes in specPerf. The website's BTU Output row gives the same 22,563 figure but cites CSA B415.1-10 where the manual cites CSA B415.1:22 (p. 4); the note quotes it as printed. Outside Air '4", meets R2000' gives one size where the manual gives 4" for runs under 25' and 5" for longer runs (p. 16); noted in specAir with 'Install to the manual.' The website's framing dimensions (45" W x 44 1/4" H x 24" D) match numbers in the Figure 2 framing drawing (p. 12), which the guide doesn't transcribe. Website rows the manual doesn't cover are not shown: shipping weight, glass viewing size, firebox size, firewood length, heating capacity, EPA average CO, the '44% cleaner' claim and the Smart BurnRate name. No in-manual conflicts were recorded, so there were no Confirm boxes to reclassify.
